## Learning Objectives
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Eigenvalues and eigenvectors are an astonishing way to understand a square matrix $A$. The idea is simple: follow the eigenvectors.

In those special directions, $A$ acts like a single number, the eigenvalue of $A.$

<br>

Today we will first introduce the concepts of eigenvalues and eigenvectors and then talk about their computation.

<br>

We will continue our discussion of these important concepts in the next lecture
:::


## The value of Eigenvalues

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
* Better understanding of Markov Chains

* Concepts required for the PageRank algorithm and principle component analysis (PCA).

## Eigenvectors

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
To explain eigenvalues, we first explain eigenvectors. 

Almost all vectors change direction, when they are multiplied by a matrix $A$. Certain exceptional vectors $\bar{x}$ are in the same direction as $A \bar{x}$. 

Those are the **eigenvectors.** Multiply an eigenvector $\bar{x}$ by $A,$ and the vector $A \bar{x}$ is a number $\lambda$ times $\bar{x}.$

<br>

:::{.center-text style="font-size: 1em"}
Consider $A = \begin{bmatrix}3&-2\\1&0\end{bmatrix}, \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix}-1\\1\end{bmatrix}, \mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}.$
:::

The images of $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ under multiplication by $A$ are shown geometrically here.

<br>

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="blue-box">
        <p>
        Are \(\bar{u}\) and \(\bar{v}\) in the same direction as \(A \bar{u}\) and \(A \bar{v}\), respectively?
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```
:::

## Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>
        An <b>eigenvector</b> of an \(n\times n\) matrix \(A\) is a nonzero vector \(\mathbf{x}\) such that \(A\mathbf{x} = \lambda\mathbf{x}\) for some scalar \(\lambda.\) The scalar \(\lambda\) is an <b>eigenvalue</b> of \(A\).
        <br><br>
        The set of all eigenvectors corresponding to a particular eigenvalue \(\lambda\) is called the <b>eigenspace of \(A\) corresponding to \(\lambda\)</b>.
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

<br>

The eigenvalue $\lambda$ tells whether the eigenvector $\bar{x}$ is streched or shrunk or reversed or left unchanged - when it is multiplied by $A.$

We may find $\lambda = 2$ or $\frac{1}{2}$ or $-1$ or $1$. The eigenvalue $\lambda$ could be zero!
:::

## Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
__Example.__  Let $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&6\\5&2\end{bmatrix}, \mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix}6\\-5\end{bmatrix}, \mathbf{v}=\begin{bmatrix}3\\-2\end{bmatrix}.$  

Are $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{v}$ eigenvectors of $A$?

__Solution.__

$$
A\mathbf{u} = \begin{bmatrix}1&6\\5&2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}6\\-5\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-24\\20\end{bmatrix} = -4\begin{bmatrix}6\\-5\end{bmatrix} = -4\mathbf{u}.
$$

$$
A\mathbf{v} = \begin{bmatrix}1&6\\5&2\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}3\\-2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-9\\11\end{bmatrix} \neq \lambda\begin{bmatrix}3\\-2\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So $\mathbf{u}$ is an eigenvector corresponding to the eigenvalue $-4$, but $\mathbf{v}$ is not an eigenvector of $A$.
:::

```{python}
        </p>

html_content = generate_html()
```

## Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
__Example.__   Show that 7 is an eigenvalue of the matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&6\\5&2\end{bmatrix}$, and find the corresponding eigenvectors.

<br>

For 7 to be an eigenvalue of $A$, it must be the case that 

$$ 
A\mathbf{x}=7\mathbf{x}
$$

has a nontrivial solution.

<br>

This is equivalent to:

$$ 
A\mathbf{x} - 7\mathbf{x} = {\bf 0}
$$

$$
A\mathbf{x} - 7I\mathbf{x} = {\bf 0}
$$

$$
(A - 7I)\mathbf{x} = {\bf 0}.
$$

:::

## Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
To solve this homogeneous equation, form the matrix

$$
A - 7I = \begin{bmatrix}1&6\\5&2\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}7&0\\0&7\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}-6&6\\5&-5\end{bmatrix}.
$$

$A-7I$ is a square matrix whose columns are linearly dependent, so by the IMT it follows that $(A - 7I)\mathbf{x} = {\bf 0}$ has a nontrivial solution.

So 7 is an eigenvalue of $A$.

To find the corresponding eigenvectors, we solve $(A - 7I)\mathbf{x} = {\bf 0}$ using row operations:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}-6&6&0\\5&-5&0\end{array}\right]
\sim\left[\begin{array}{cc|c}1&-1&0\\0&0&0\end{array}\right].
$$

This says that $x_1 = x_2,$ and $x_2$ is free.

So the general solution has the form $x_2\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}.$  

Each vector of this form with $x_2 \neq 0$ is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda = 7.$
:::

## Finding the Eigenspace

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
From the previous example, we can conclude that $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of an $n\times n$ matrix $A$ if and only if the equation

$$
(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{x} = {\bf 0}
$$

has a nontrivial solution.

<br>

As a result, the _eigenspace_ (i.e., the set of all eigenvectors) of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda$ is just __the null space of the matrix $A-\lambda I.$__ That is, the eigenvectors make up the null space of $A-\lambda I.$

Hence, it is a subspace. 

Recall from the Rank Theorem that the dimension of a null space (and therefore of an eigenspace) can be anywhere from $0$ to $n$.

<br>

If $A$ is the identity matrix in $\mathbb{R}^{2 \times 2}$, all vectors in $\mathbb{R^2}$ are its eigenvectors. The only eigenvalue of $I$ is 1. This is unusual. Most $2 \times 2$ matrices have 2 eigenvector directions and 2 eigenvalues.

:::

## Finding the Eigenspace

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
__Example.__  For matrix $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&6\\5&2\end{bmatrix}$,

- We found that the general solution for the eigenvector corrsponding to $\lambda = 7$ is the expression $x_2\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix}.$  

- This means that the eigenspace of $A$ corresponding to $\lambda = 7$ consists of all multiples of $\begin{bmatrix}1\\1\end{bmatrix},$ which is the line through $(1,1)$ and the origin.

We could also show that the eigenspace corresponding to $\lambda = -4$ is the line through $(-6, 5)$.
:::

## Finding the Eigenspace

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
```{python}
#
ax = ut.plotSetup(-10,10,-6,10,size=(12,8))
ut.centerAxes(ax)
A = np.array([[1,6],[5,2]])
u = np.array([1,1])
v = np.array([3./2,-5./4])
#
ax.plot(v[0],v[1],'bo')
ax.plot(A.dot(v)[0],A.dot(v)[1],'bo')

ax.text(A.dot(v)[0]+0.2,A.dot(v)[1]+0.2,r'$A{\bf v}$',size=20)
ax.plot([-10,10],[5*10/6.0,-5*10/6.0],'b-',lw=2)
#
ax.plot(u[0],u[1],'ro')
ax.plot(A.dot(u)[0],A.dot(u)[1],'ro')
ax.text(u[0]+0.7,u[1],r'${\bf u}$',size=20)
ax.text(A.dot(u)[0]+0.7,A.dot(u)[1],r'$A{\bf u}$',size=20)

# 
ax.annotate('', xy=(A.dot(u)[0], A.dot(u)[1]),  xycoords='data',
                xytext=(u[0], u[1]), textcoords='data',
                size=18,
                #bbox=dict(boxstyle="round", fc="0.8"),
```

## Finding the Eigenspace

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
We can also find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&6\\5&2\end{bmatrix}$ using `numpy`.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: true
A = np.array([[4, -1, 6],
              [2,  1, 6],
              [2, -1, 8]])
for i in range(len(A)):
    print("eigenvalue", np.round(np.linalg.eigvals(A)[i]), "with eigenvector", np.round(np.linalg.eig(A)[1][:,i], 5))
```

<br>

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
In general, when we know the eigenvalue $\lambda,$ we find the eigenvector by solving $(A-\lambda I) \bar{x} = \bar{0}$
:::

## Finding the Eigenspace

:::{style="font-size: .5em"}
__Example.__  Let $A = \begin{bmatrix}4&-1&6\\2&1&6\\2&-1&8\end{bmatrix}.$  An eigenvalue of $A$ is $2.$  Find a basis for the the corresponding eigenspace.

<br>

__Solution.__  The eigenspace we are looking for is the nullspace of

$$
A - 2I = \begin{bmatrix}4&-1&6\\2&1&6\\2&-1&8\end{bmatrix}-\begin{bmatrix}2&0&0\\0&2&0\\0&0&2\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2&-1&6\\2&-1&6\\2&-1&6\end{bmatrix}.
$$

<br>

Let's row reduce the augmented matrix for $(A-2I)\mathbf{x}={\bf 0}$:

$$
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}2&-1&6&0\\2&-1&6&0\\2&-1&6&0\end{array}\right]
\sim
\left[\begin{array}{ccc|c}1&-1/2&3&0\\0&0&0&0\\0&0&0&0\end{array}\right]
$$

At this point, it is clear that 2 is indeed an eigenvalue of $A$ because the equation $(A-2I)\mathbf{x} = {\bf 0}$ has free variables.
:::

## Finding the Eigenspace

:::{style="font-size: .6em"}
- All solutions lie on the plane $x_1 = \frac{1}{2}x_2 +-3x_3.$

- Expressed as a vector, the general solution is: $\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}x_2 - 3x_3\\x_2\\x_3\end{bmatrix}.$

- Expressed as a vector sum, this is: $x_2\begin{bmatrix}1/2\\1\\0\end{bmatrix} + x_3\begin{bmatrix}-3\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}$ with $x_2$ and $x_3$ free.

<br>

So this eigenspace is a two-dimensional subspace of $\mathbb{R}^3,$ and a basis for this subspace is

$$
\left\{\begin{bmatrix}1/2\\1\\0\end{bmatrix},\begin{bmatrix}-3\\0\\1\end{bmatrix}\right\}.
$$

:::

## Finding the Eigenvalues

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
How do we find the eigenvalues?

If $(A- \lambda I)\mathbf{x} = {\bf 0}$ has a nonzero solution, $A - \lambda I$ is not invertible. By the IMT, the determinant of $A - \lambda I$ must be zero.

<br>

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p>
        The scalar \(\lambda\) is an eigenvalue of \(A\) if and only if \(A - \lambda I\) is singular (i.e., \(\operatorname{det}(A - \lambda I) = 0\))
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

<br>

For any $n \times n$ matrix, $\operatorname{det}(A - \lambda I)$ is a polynomial of degree $n,$ called the __characteristic polynomial__ of $A.$

The equation $\operatorname{det}(A - \lambda I)$ is known as the __characteristic equation.__
:::


## Finding the Eigenvalues

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
__Example.__  Find the eigenvalues of $A = \begin{bmatrix}2&3\\3&-6\end{bmatrix}.$

<br>

__Solution.__  We must find all scalars $\lambda$ such that the matrix equation

$$
(A-\lambda I)\mathbf{x} = {\bf 0}
$$

has a nontrivial solution. This problem is equivalent to finding all $\lambda$ such that the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is _not_ invertible, or equivalently, $\operatorname{det}(A - \lambda I).$

$$
A - \lambda I = \begin{bmatrix}2&3\\3&-6\end{bmatrix} - \begin{bmatrix}\lambda&0\\0&\lambda\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}2-\lambda&3\\3&-6-\lambda\end{bmatrix}.
$$

So the eigenvalues of $A$ are the solutions of the characteristic equation
:::

## Finding the Eigenvalues

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
$$
\begin{eqnarray*}
0 &=& \det(A-\lambda I) \\
&=& \det\begin{bmatrix}2-\lambda&3\\3&-6-\lambda\end{bmatrix} \\
&=& (2-\lambda)(-6-\lambda)-(3)(3) \\
&=& -12 + 6\lambda -2\lambda + \lambda^2 - 9 \\
&=& \lambda^2+4\lambda-21 \\
&=& (\lambda-3)(\lambda + 7)
\end{eqnarray*}
$$

If $\det(A-\lambda I) = 0,$ then $\lambda = 3$ or $\lambda = -7.$  So the eigenvalues of $A$ are $3$ and $-7$.
:::

## Finding the Eigenvalues

:::{style="font-size: .5em"}
__Example.__  Find the characteristic equation of 

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}5&-2&6&-1\\0&3&-8&0\\0&0&5&4\\0&0&0&1\end{bmatrix}
$$

__Solution.__  Form $A - \lambda I,$ and note that $\det A$ is the product of the entries on the diagonal of $A,$ if $A$ is triangular.

$$
\det(A-\lambda I) = \det\begin{bmatrix}5-\lambda&-2&6&-1\\0&3-\lambda&-8&0\\0&0&5-\lambda&4\\0&0&0&1-\lambda\end{bmatrix}
$$

$$
=(5-\lambda)(3-\lambda)(5-\lambda)(1-\lambda).
$$

<br>

So the characteristic equation is: $\begin{eqnarray*}(\lambda-5)^2(\lambda-3)(\lambda-1) &=& 0 \\ \lambda^4 - 14\lambda^3 + 68 \lambda^2 - 130\lambda + 75 &=& 0. \end{eqnarray*}$
:::


## Finding the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors{.really-really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: 1.5em"}
In summary, to find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of an $n \times n$ matrix $A,$ we follow these steps.

1. _Compute the determinant of $A - \lambda I$_.<br>
 With $\lambda$ subtracted along the diagonal, this determinant starts with $\lambda^n$ or $- \lambda^n.$ It is a polynomial in $\lambda$ of degree $n.$

2. _Find the roots of this polynomial_ by solving $\operatorname{det}(A - \lambda I)=0.$ The $n$ roots are the $n$ eigenvalues of $A.$ They make $A - \lambda I$ singular.

3. For each eigenvalue $\lambda,$ solve $(A - \lambda I)\bar{x}=0$ _to find an eigenvector $\bar{x}$_
:::


## Finding the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors{.really-really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: 1.5em"}
Let $A = \begin{bmatrix}1&2\\2&4\end{bmatrix}.$ Find its eigenvalues and eigenvectors.

1. $A - \lambda I = \begin{bmatrix}1- \lambda &2\\2&4 - \lambda \end{bmatrix}$ <br>$\operatorname{det}(A - \lambda I) = (1 - \lambda)(4 - \lambda) - (2)(2) = \lambda^2 - 5 \lambda$

<br>

2. Set this determinant to zero:<br>$\lambda^2 - 5 \lambda = \lambda(\lambda - 5) = 0.$ <br>Hence, the eigenvalues of $A$ are $\lambda_1=0$ and $\lambda_2=5.$
:::


## Finding the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors{.really-really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: 1.2em"}

3. It remains to find the eigenvectors. Solve $\operatorname{det}(A - \lambda I) = 0$ seperately for $\lambda_1 = 0$ and $\lambda_2=5.$

$$
\left[ A - 0I \,\middle|\, \bar{0} \right] = 
\left[ \begin{array}{cc|c}
1 & 2 & 0 \\
2 & 4 & 0
\end{array} \right]
\sim
\left[ \begin{array}{cc|c}
1 & 2 & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{array} \right].
$$

$x_2$ is free, $x_1$ is equal to $-2x_2.$ Let $x_2=-1$. Then $\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}$ is an eigenvector for $\lambda_1 = 0.$

$$
\left[ A - 5I \,\middle|\, \bar{0} \right] = 
\left[ \begin{array}{cc|c}
-4 & 2 & 0 \\
2 & -1 & 0
\end{array} \right]
\sim
\left[ \begin{array}{cc|c}
1 & -\frac{1}{2} & 0 \\
0 & 0 & 0
\end{array} \right].
$$

Hence, $\begin{bmatrix}1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}$ is an eigenvector for $\lambda_2$ = 5.
:::

## Finding the Eigenvalues and Eigenvectors{.really-really-smaller-title}

:::{style="font-size: 1.5em"}
```{python}

        Let \(A=\begin{bmatrix}2&1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\). Find the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of \(A\).
        </p>
```

## Key Ideas

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

* $A \bar{x} = \lambda \bar{x}$ says that eigenvectors $\bar{x}$ keep the same direction when multiplied by $A.$
* $A \bar{x} = \lambda \bar{x}$ also says that $\operatorname{det}(A - \lambda I)=0$. This determines $n$ eigenvalues
* The eigenvectors corresponding to an eigenvalue $\lambda$ are found directly from $(A-\lambda I) \bar{x} = \bar{0}$.
:::
